summary.text: Letting $A=2^{2^{33}}$, any admissible $m<2A$ has $\varphi(m)=A$; even $m$ are excluded by $2\varphi(m)\le m$, while for odd $m$ the totient product formula forces $m$ to be a squarefree product of distinct Fermat primes with $\sum_{i\in S}2^i=2^{33}$, so uniqueness of binary expansion gives $S=\{33\}$ and hence $m=F_{33}$ with $F_{33}$ prime. Thus if $F_{33}$ is composite the first possible value is $2A$, whose totient is $A$, whereas if it is prime then $\varphi(F_{33})=A$ and no smaller $m<F_{33}=A+1$ can work because $\varphi(m)<m$ for $m>1$.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
N=2^{33},\qquad A=2^N=2^{2^{33}},\qquad F=F_{33}=2^{2^{33}}+1=A+1,
\]
and let
\[
B=2^{N+1}=2^{2^{33}+1}=2A.
\]
By definition, \(a(N)\) is the least positive integer \(m\) such that
\[
A=2^N\mid \varphi(m).
\]
We prove that
\[
a(N)=
\begin{cases}
F,&\text{if }F\text{ is prime},\\
B,&\text{if }F\text{ is not prime}.
\end{cases}
\]

We first establish the auxiliary facts needed to control every admissible integer below \(B\).

### 1. Totients of even integers

We shall use the inequality
\[
2\varphi(m)\le m \tag{1}
\]
for every even nonnegative integer \(m\).

Write \(m=2n\). This can be proved by induction on \(m\), or equivalently by repeatedly removing factors of \(2\). If \(n=0\), the assertion is immediate. Suppose \(n>0\).

If \(n\) is even, then
\[
\varphi(2n)=2\varphi(n).
\]
Indeed, in this case multiplying \(n\) by another factor of \(2\) doubles its totient. Applying the inductive inequality \(2\varphi(n)\le n\), we obtain
\[
2\varphi(2n)=4\varphi(n)\le 2n=m.
\]

If \(n\) is odd, then
\[
\varphi(2n)=\varphi(n),
\]
because adjoining a single factor \(2\), coprime to odd \(n\), does not change the totient. Since the elementary bound \(\varphi(n)\le n\) always holds,
\[
2\varphi(2n)=2\varphi(n)\le 2n=m.
\]
Thus (1) holds for every even \(m\).

### 2. Divisibility forces exact equality below \(B\)

Suppose that \(m>0\), that \(A\mid\varphi(m)\), and that \(m<B=2A\). Since \(m>0\), its totient is positive. We may therefore write
\[
\varphi(m)=Ac
\]
with a positive integer \(c\). On the other hand,
\[
Ac=\varphi(m)\le m<2A.
\]
Since \(A>0\), this gives \(c<2\). Hence \(c=1\), and therefore
\[
\varphi(m)=A. \tag{2}
\]

Moreover, every such \(m\) is odd. For if it were even, (1) and (2) would give
\[
B=2A=2\varphi(m)\le m,
\]
contrary to \(m<B\). We have proved:

> If \(m>0\), \(A\mid\varphi(m)\), and \(m<B\), then \(\varphi(m)=A\) and \(m\) is odd.

### 3. Classification of an integer below \(B\) with totient \(A\)

We now prove the central assertion:

> If \(m>0\), \(m<B\), and \(\varphi(m)=A\), then \(m=F\), and in particular \(F\) is prime.

Let \(\mathcal P\) be the finite set of distinct prime divisors of \(m\), and define
\[
P=\prod_{p\in\mathcal P}p,
\qquad
Q=\prod_{p\in\mathcal P}(p-1).
\]
Euler’s product formula, grouped according to the distinct prime factors, says
\[
\varphi(m)=\frac{m}{P}\,Q. \tag{3}
\]
For completeness, if
\[
m=\prod_{p\in\mathcal P}p^{e_p},
\]
then
\[
\varphi(m)=\prod_{p\in\mathcal P}p^{e_p-1}(p-1),
\]
and \(m/P=\prod p^{e_p-1}\), which gives (3).

By the result of the previous section, \(m\) is odd. Since \(P\mid m\), the quotient \(m/P\) is also odd. Equation (3), together with \(\varphi(m)=A\), shows that \(m/P\) divides \(A=2^N\). The only odd divisor of a power of \(2\) is \(1\), so
\[
\frac mP=1.
\]
Consequently,
\[
m=P \tag{4}
\]
and, from (3),
\[
Q=A. \tag{5}
\]
Thus \(m\) is squarefree, and the product of \(p-1\) over its distinct prime factors is exactly \(A\).

Fix a prime \(p\mid m\). Because \(m\) is odd, \(p\ne2\). By (5), \(p-1\mid A=2^N\). Every divisor of a power of \(2\) is itself a power of \(2\), so
\[
p-1=2^r
\]
for some integer \(r\ge0\). Since \(p\ne2\), we cannot have \(r=0\). Thus \(r>0\), and
\[
p=2^r+1. \tag{6}
\]
Because \(p\) is prime, the exponent \(r\) must itself be a power of \(2\). Here is the standard elementary argument. Write
\[
r=2^i u
\]
where \(u\) is odd. If \(u>1\), then, setting \(x=2^{2^i}>1\), we have
\[
2^r+1=x^u+1.
\]
For odd \(u\), \(x+1\) divides \(x^u+1\). When \(u>1\), this is a proper nontrivial divisor, contradicting the primality of \(2^r+1\). Therefore \(u=1\), so \(r=2^i\). Equation (6) becomes
\[
p=2^{2^i}+1=F_i.
\]
Hence every prime divisor of \(m\) is a Fermat number which is itself prime.

For each prime divisor \(p\) of \(m\), choose an index \(i(p)\) such that
\[
p=F_{i(p)}=2^{2^{i(p)}}+1.
\]
Distinct prime divisors have distinct chosen indices: if \(i(p)=i(q)\), then both \(p\) and \(q\) equal the same Fermat number, hence \(p=q\). Let
\[
S=\{i(p):p\in\mathcal P\}.
\]
Using (5), we calculate
\[
A=Q
 =\prod_{p\in\mathcal P}(p-1)
 =\prod_{p\in\mathcal P}2^{2^{i(p)}}
 =2^{\sum_{p\in\mathcal P}2^{i(p)}}
 =2^{\sum_{i\in S}2^i}.
\]
Since \(A=2^{2^{33}}\) and powers of \(2\) have unique exponents,
\[
\sum_{i\in S}2^i=2^{33}. \tag{7}
\]

We now use the uniqueness of binary expansion in the particularly simple form needed here. Equation (7) forces
\[
S=\{33\}. \tag{8}
\]
Indeed, no \(i>33\) can belong to \(S\), because its single summand \(2^i\) would already exceed \(2^{33}\). If \(33\in S\), then the summand \(2^{33}\) already equals the entire sum, and positivity of all other summands shows that there can be no other element. If \(33\notin S\), then \(S\subseteq\{0,1,\ldots,32\}\), and therefore
\[
\sum_{i\in S}2^i\le\sum_{i=0}^{32}2^i=2^{33}-1,
\]
contradicting (7). This proves (8).

It follows that the set of prime divisors of \(m\) is exactly \(\{F_{33}\}\). It is nonempty because its index set is the nonempty set \(\{33\}\). By (4), \(m\) is the product of its distinct prime divisors, and hence
\[
m=F_{33}=F.
\]
Furthermore, every member of the prime-divisor set is prime, so \(F_{33}\) is prime. This proves the central classification.

### 4. The two universal candidates

First observe that
\[
F=A+1<2A=B, \tag{9}
\]
because \(A>1\).

We claim that \(F\) is admissible, meaning \(A\mid\varphi(F)\), exactly when \(F\) is prime.

If \(F\) is prime, then
\[
\varphi(F)=F-1=A,
\]
so it is admissible.

Conversely, suppose \(F\) is admissible. It is positive and, by (9), lies below \(B\). Section 2 then gives \(\varphi(F)=A=F-1\). A positive integer \(n\) satisfies \(\varphi(n)=n-1\) exactly when it is prime: for a prime, every positive residue below it is coprime to it; for a composite \(n>1\), a proper nontrivial divisor is one of the residues below \(n\) that is not coprime to \(n\) (and \(n=1\) plainly does not satisfy the equality). Thus \(F\) is prime.

The number \(B\) is always admissible. Indeed,
\[
B=2^{N+1},

giving
\[
\varphi(B)=\varphi(2^{N+1})=2^N=A.
\]
Therefore the defining set for \(a(N)\) is nonempty in both cases.

### 5. Minimality when \(F\) is prime

Assume first that \(F\) is prime. As just shown, \(F\) is admissible. We prove that no smaller positive integer is admissible.

Suppose, toward a contradiction, that \(m<F=A+1\) is positive and admissible. Since \(F<B\), we have \(m<B\), and Section 2 gives
\[
\varphi(m)=A. \tag{10}
\]
The general inequality \(\varphi(m)\le m\) gives \(A\le m\), while \(m<A+1\) gives \(m\le A\). Thus one could already conclude \(m=A\). But \(A>1\), and for every integer \(m>1\) one has the strict inequality \(\varphi(m)<m\): the residue represented by any nontrivial common factor, or simply the residue \(m\) in the usual count from \(1\) through \(m\), ensures not all residues are counted as coprime; equivalently this follows immediately from Euler’s product formula. Here \(A\le m\) ensures \(m>1\), so (10) yields
\[
A=\varphi(m)<m.
\]
Hence \(A+1\le m\), contradicting \(m<A+1\). Therefore every admissible positive integer is at least \(F\), and since \(F\) itself is admissible,
\[
a(N)=F
\]
when \(F\) is prime.

### 6. Minimality when \(F\) is composite

Now assume that \(F\) is not prime. The number \(B\) is admissible, so \(a(N)\le B\). Suppose there were an admissible positive integer \(m<B\). Section 2 would give
\[
\varphi(m)=A,
\]
and Section 3 would then imply both
\[
m=F
\quad\text{and}\quad
F\text{ is prime}.
\]
This contradicts the present assumption that \(F\) is not prime. Thus no admissible positive integer lies below \(B\). Since \(B\) itself is admissible, it is the least one, and
\[
a(N)=B=2^{N+1}
\]
when \(F\) is composite.

Substituting \(N=2^{33}\) and \(F=F_{33}\), we conclude
\[
\boxed{
a(2^{33})=
\begin{cases}
F_{33}=2^{2^{33}}+1,&\text{if }F_{33}\text{ is prime},\\[2mm]
2^{2^{33}+1},&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}}
\]
